newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. envoy meets Iraqi officials.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy meets Iraqi officials.

text.p: United Nations arms envoy Rolf Ekeus held talks with senior Iraqi officials in Baghdad on Friday in an attempt to resolve a number of disputes over Iraq's weapons programme, a U.N. official said.

Ekeus, head of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) disarming Iraq under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire terms, arrived in Baghdad on Thursday in a bid to defuse a stand-off over wrecked missile engines which his commission would like to remove to the United States for analysis.

Roger Knight, assistant director of Baghdad's UNSCOM Ongoing Monitoring and Verification Centre, told Reuters that Ekeus met Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz, Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed and Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf.
"Talks centre on chemical and missile issues," he said without giving further details.
Ekeus had met Aziz shortly after he arrived in Baghdad on Thursday and the official Iraqi News Agency said a third round of talks was set for later on Friday.
Iraq's ruling Baath Party newspaper al-Thawra said the authorities "are trying to answer all Ekeus's questions and offer him all the information (on Iraq's weapons)".
Thawra maintained an anti-Ekeus campaign in Baghdad's press, accusing him of carrying out an anti-Iraq policy drawn up by the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA).

"Nothing has remained (for Iraq to do) but Mr Ekeus's suspicions and aggressive suggestions and question marks which are drawn up by the CIA and other parties...in order to prolong the (U.N.) embargo on Iraq," it said in a front-page editorial.
Ekeus believes Iraq still has a significant number of operational missiles which could constitute a complete rocket force. Iraq has denied the accusation.
Thawra said "Iraq does not conceal missiles or information as it is alleged by Ekeus...not to appease him or anybody else but in order to speed up an end to the suffering of our people".

Sanctions imposed on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait can be lifted only when Ekeus's commission decides that Iraq has scrapped all of its weapons of mass destruction including missiles with ranges greater than 150 km (95 miles).
The paper said Ekeus's "allegation that Iraq still hides missiles is untrue whatsoever...aiming at creating excuses in order not to close (Iraq's) weapons files."
Ekeus is accompanied by a team of 10 international experts on ballastic missiles and chemical arms including Russian missile expert Nikita Smidovich.
Iraq has begun since January excavations to recover what it said were missile components destroyed soon after the 1991 Gulf War which drove Iraqi troops out of Kuwait.
